strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: combining multi-omic measurements, biomedical graphs, and language models for interpretable cancer dependency prediction.
Using a pretrained graph classifier to guide incremental subgraph construction is an interesting application of process-level supervision that avoids manually annotated reasoning trajectories.

GALAX improves aggregate performance over the strongest task-tuned LLM baseline: F1 increases from 0.5094 to 0.5399, recall from 0.4959 to 0.5332, and Hit@5 from 0.8889 to 0.9249. The appendix provides cohort-level results, training details, and illustrative enrichment analyses.
weaknesses: The central reward is insufficiently validated. The GNN predicts cancerous versus non-cancerous status, whereas the downstream task ranks gene dependencies within cancer cell lines. High classification accuracy does not establish that its scores measure intermediate reasoning correctness, essentiality, or mechanistic plausibility. Its behavior on generated partial graphs, including susceptibility to reward exploitation, is not evaluated.

Equation 12 appears to reverse the intended policy update. With conventional nonnegative cross-entropy, minimizing negative reward times cross-entropy reduces the probability of positively rewarded actions. The authors must clarify the convention and implementation; as written, the objective contradicts the claimed reinforcement mechanism.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed mechanism. GALAX receives an additional supervised fine-tuning stage, but there is no matched additional-training baseline without generated graphs, nor comparisons against random or greedy subgraph selection. Ablations removing classifier rewards, rollout rewards, rule rewards, and omic conditioning are missing. The modest gains therefore cannot confidently be attributed to process supervision.

The benchmark does not adequately establish personalization. Top-100 dependency lists may contain many shared essential genes, yet training-set frequency rankings, mean-dependency rankings, disease-only predictors, and omics-shuffling controls are absent. The near-zero performance of the supervised GAT baseline also requires investigation and stronger conventional dependency-prediction comparisons.

Evaluation is small and inconsistently documented. The dataset contains 363 cell lines, with only 63 test examples in the appendix and one or two examples for several cancers. The stated 80/20 split conflicts with the reported 300/63 partition; four experimental seeds are described alongside five-trial checkpoint selection. Appendix C.3 explicitly selects the graph classifier checkpoint using test accuracy, compromising that reported generalization estimate. No independent cohort or held-out cancer-type evaluation supports broader generalization.

The claims of consistent superiority and statistical significance exceed the results. For example, GALAX underperforms task-tuned baselines on several cohorts, including STAD and PRAD, and no significance tests are supplied. Hit@K is not formally defined; figures label the corresponding quantities precision@K, and Hit@5 frequently exceeds Hit@10, making the metric interpretation ambiguous.

Explainability is supported primarily by pathway enrichment of graphs already initialized using disease-associated knowledge. Without enrichment comparisons against the retrieved starting graphs and appropriate random controls, this does not establish new mechanistic insight. There are no faithfulness tests showing that the final LLM uses the generated edges. Cell-line essentiality also does not establish selective therapeutic benefit or patient-specific clinical utility.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims remain incomplete. The supplied manuscript leaves the advertised repository and dataset links blank, omits important reward and entity-extraction implementation details, and gives a complexity analysis that suppresses repeated graph construction, rollouts, and retries without reporting runtime or memory measurements.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: integrating quantitative omics, biomedical graphs, and language models for target prioritization. Constructing explicit subgraphs offers a useful, inspectable intermediate representation.

Target-QA combines multi-omic inputs with experimentally derived CRISPR dependency labels across 363 cell lines. The appendix provides substantial information about data sources, prompts, architectures, and training settings.

GALAX improves reported aggregate performance over task-finetuned LLaMA3: precision increases from 0.5250 to 0.5472, recall from 0.4959 to 0.5332, and F1 from 0.5094 to 0.5399. Comparisons include static graph augmentation and an adapted G-Retriever.
The subgraph visualizations and enrichment analyses provide qualitative evidence of biological relevance, including adjusted significance values and acknowledgment of some nonsignificant findings.
weaknesses: The central reward lacks validation for its intended purpose. The GNN predicts binary cancerous versus non-cancerous status, but its confidence on partially constructed subgraphs is treated as evidence of correct reasoning and target relevance. Neither whole-graph classification accuracy nor edge-prediction AUC establishes this connection. There is no demonstrated relationship between reward, CRISPR dependency prediction, and intermediate biological correctness, or assessment of reward exploitation under subgraph distribution shift.

Equation 12 has an apparent optimization-sign error. With conventional cross-entropy CE = -log p, minimizing -R × CE decreases the probability of positively rewarded actions. Reward-weighted cross-entropy should instead have a positive coefficient, equivalently minimizing -R log p. The authors need to reconcile the equation with the implementation; as written, the central training objective contradicts its stated purpose.

The evaluation does not establish personalization. Ranking the strongest CRISPR dependencies can reward predicting broadly essential genes shared across cell lines. Missing controls include training-set gene-frequency or mean-dependency rankings, disease-only inputs, shuffled omics, and conventional supervised dependency predictors. The near-zero GAT baseline also warrants diagnostic checks. Without these comparisons, strong absolute performance could largely reflect shared target frequencies rather than sample-specific reasoning.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed contribution. GALAX receives additional final-stage supervised finetuning, while the strongest QA baseline does not clearly receive matched training. There are no controlled comparisons against random or heuristic subgraphs, terminal-only rewards, or removal of the classifier, rollout, and rule components. Consequently, the modest incremental gains cannot confidently be attributed to graph process supervision.

Model selection and experimental reporting undermine confidence. Appendix C.3 explicitly selects the graph classifier checkpoint using test accuracy, compromising that held-out estimate. The reported 80/20 Target-QA split is actually 300/63, or 82.6/17.4%; four evaluation seeds are described alongside five training trials and best-run selection without a clear account of their relationship. Independent validation and consistent split/checkpoint protocols are needed.

Generalization and superiority claims exceed the evidence. Evaluation uses one small benchmark, with only seven LUAD and six BRCA test samples and still smaller remaining cohorts; there is no external or held-out-cancer evaluation. Paired significance tests are absent despite claims of significant improvement. The claim of outperforming every baseline on every metric is contradicted by BRCA Hit@10 and several appendix results, including GBM, STAD, and PRAD.

Interpretability is demonstrated as plausibility rather than faithfulness. Disease-associated genes and known interactions already enter candidate selection and reward constraints, so subsequent disease/pathway enrichment is not independent validation. The paper lacks matched enrichment controls and tests showing that selected edges are necessary or sufficient for the final prediction. Cell-line essentiality also does not establish patient-specific therapeutic selectivity or clinical utility.

Efficiency and evaluation details remain incomplete. The complexity analysis suppresses graph-construction steps, repeated rollouts, retries, and policy optimization without runtime or memory measurements. Hit@k is not precisely defined and is labeled precision@k in figures; GPT-4o-mini entity extraction lacks an accuracy audit. These omissions limit reproducibility and interpretation of the reported gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: combining quantitative multi-omics, biomedical graph structure, and language models for target prioritization with inspectable subgraph evidence.
Using a pretrained graph classifier to guide incremental subgraph construction is an interesting approach to obtaining intermediate supervision without manually annotated reasoning trajectories.

GALAX reports improvements over the strongest QA-tuned baseline: overall precision increases from 0.5250 to 0.5472, recall from 0.4959 to 0.5332, and F1 from 0.5094 to 0.5399. The appendices provide extensive cohort-level results, training details, and biological enrichment examples.
weaknesses: The central reward is insufficiently validated. The GNN predicts cancerous versus non-cancerous status, not target essentiality or intermediate reasoning correctness. Its classification accuracy on complete graphs does not establish that its confidence on generated partial graphs measures biological plausibility or useful target-selection steps. Reward calibration, correlation with downstream accuracy, and susceptibility to reward exploitation are not evaluated.

Equation 12 appears to have the wrong optimization sign. With conventional positive cross-entropy, minimizing minus reward times cross-entropy reduces the probability of positively rewarded actions. The authors need to correct the equation or clarify the implementation and objective convention; this directly affects the central algorithm.

The benchmark does not establish personalized prediction. Top-100 CRISPR dependencies can include broadly essential genes, but there are no training-set frequency, mean-essentiality, disease-only, or shuffled-omics controls. Evaluation excluding common essentials and testing unseen cancer types would help distinguish cell-specific reasoning from learning shared target lists. Cancer-cell essentiality also does not by itself establish therapeutic selectivity or patient-level utility.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed contribution. GALAX receives additional final-stage fine-tuning, but there is no matched-training control without generated graphs, or comparison against random or greedy subgraph construction. Ablations removing classifier reward, rollout reward, and rule constraints are missing. The near-zero GAT results require stronger implementation validation and comparison with competitive supervised dependency-prediction methods.

Evaluation integrity and reporting need clarification. Appendix C.3 explicitly selects the graph-classifier checkpoint using test accuracy, compromising that reported generalization estimate. The stated 80/20 split conflicts with the reported 300/63 division, and four-seed evaluation is difficult to reconcile with five trials and best-run selection elsewhere. No separate validation protocol or paired significance analysis is provided. Many cancer-specific test cohorts contain only one to three samples.

Explanation quality is supported mainly by enrichment of subgraphs already seeded from disease-associated knowledge. Without comparisons to the initial retrieved graph and size- or degree-matched controls, this provides limited independent validation. There are no quantitative faithfulness, deletion, stability, or counterfactual tests showing that the displayed subgraphs explain the final LLM predictions.

Several claims exceed the evidence. GALAX does not outperform every baseline on every metric, including BRCA Hit@10 and multiple appendix results. Hit@k is undefined and appears as precision@k in figures. The complexity analysis suppresses rollout depth, repeated classifier evaluations, retries, and graph-generation training, while providing no measured latency or memory comparison to substantiate scalability.

strengths: The integration of multi-omic features, biomedical graphs, and language models addresses a meaningful target-prioritization problem. Explicit subgraph construction provides an inspectable intermediate representation.
GALAX improves reported overall precision/recall to 0.5472/0.5332, versus 0.5250/0.4959 for the QA-tuned omics baseline. Similar results with Qwen2.5 provide some evidence of backbone robustness.

Evaluation includes several graph-augmented baselines, modality and graph perturbations, reward-component and reward-density ablations, held-out cancer types, and external pediatric data. These are useful additions beyond the main random-split experiment.
weaknesses: The central optimization equation has an unresolved sign error. Equation 12 defines the minimized loss as negative reward times cross-entropy. Under the standard cross-entropy definition, this decreases the probability of positively rewarded actions, opposite to the stated objective. The authors must clarify whether this is a notation error or reflects the implementation.

The reward's biological interpretation is insufficiently justified. A cancer-versus-noncancer classifier trained on whole graphs is applied to partial subgraphs, but its calibration under this distribution shift is not evaluated. High cancer-class probability does not establish target essentiality, causal pathway correctness, or correctness of an individual construction step. Freezing the classifier and adding rollout rewards also do not establish resistance to reward hacking.

The benchmark does not adequately distinguish cell-specific prediction from recovery of broadly essential genes. Missing controls include training-set target-frequency rankings, mean gene-effect rankings, and omics-shuffled or cell-identity-only predictors. Such controls are especially important because QA finetuning accounts for most of the improvement and the labels select the strongest viability effects rather than cancer-selective therapeutic vulnerabilities.

Evaluation and reporting contain material inconsistencies. Appendix C.3 explicitly selects the graph classifier checkpoint using test accuracy. Appendix B.3 calls a 300/63 split of 363 samples an 80/20 split. Table 11 reports F1 = 0.5336 for the no-Graph variant despite precision/recall of 0.5314/0.5275, which is inconsistent with standard F1 aggregation using the same samples and weights. Hit@K is not clearly defined, and Hit@5 exceeding Hit@10 requires clarification if these are intended as conventional hit rates.

The contribution of reinforcement-guided construction remains incompletely isolated despite the component ablations. GALAX receives an additional answer-finetuning stage; a matched two-stage baseline with random or heuristic subgraphs is needed to separate graph-search benefits from extra optimization and context. The held-out cancer-type experiments also omit baseline comparisons, limiting conclusions about comparative generalization.

The explanation evidence establishes plausibility rather than faithfulness or mechanism discovery. Enrichment and ratings of ten examples lack matched baseline subgraphs and tests showing that the identified edges drive predictions. Disease-associated starting nodes already favor disease-related enrichment. Claims about patient-specific mechanisms therefore exceed evidence from cell-line target overlap and general cancer relevance.

The scalability argument omits important costs: construction steps, repeated classifier evaluations, rollout number and length, and multiple search retries. No measured runtime comparison substantiates the claimed computational competitiveness. More generally, the architecture is a combination of established components whose distinctive benefit remains uncertain given the methodological and evaluation issues above.

strengths: The problem is important: integrating quantitative multi-omics, biological graphs, and language models for interpretable cancer dependency prediction. Target-QA provides a potentially useful benchmark built around experimental CRISPR outcomes.
GALAX offers a concrete integration of candidate generation, sequential graph construction, classifier-based rewards, and graph-conditioned answer generation.

The reported evaluation includes several relevant graph-augmented baselines, two language-model backbones, reward-component and input ablations, held-out cancer types, and an external pediatric dataset. Overall Target-QA precision/recall improve from 0.5250/0.4959 for the QA-tuned omics baseline to 0.5472/0.5332.
The appendix supplies substantial implementation detail and includes biological enrichment analyses and assessments by three bioinformaticians, providing preliminary evidence of subgraph relevance.
weaknesses: The central reward is insufficiently validated. The graph supervisor distinguishes cancerous from non-cancerous samples, whereas the downstream task ranks gene dependencies within cancer cell lines. High binary classification accuracy does not establish that scores on incrementally constructed subgraphs measure target essentiality, mechanistic correctness, or intermediate reasoning quality. Freezing this classifier and checking known edges also do not establish resistance to reward hacking.

The policy objective has an apparent sign error. Equation 12 defines the minimized loss as negative reward times cross-entropy. Under the standard cross-entropy convention, minimizing this expression decreases the probability of positively rewarded actions. The paper needs to resolve whether this is a notation error or an implementation problem; the stated algorithm does not support its intended optimization.

Personalization remains inadequately established. There is no training-set target-frequency or mean-dependency baseline to quantify how much performance comes from predicting common essential genes. Omics-removal ablations are useful but do not replace these controls or shuffled-profile tests. The held-out-cancer experiment reports only GALAX, leaving its advantage over simpler methods under distribution shift unknown. Cancer-cell essentiality alone also does not demonstrate selective therapeutic benefit or patient-specific clinical utility.

Experimental attribution and baseline adequacy are unresolved. GALAX receives an additional final-answer fine-tuning stage, but an otherwise matched two-stage baseline without the learned graph is not clearly established. The nearly zero supervised GAT performance warrants investigation rather than attribution to absent global reasoning. Appendix D.3 also introduces GPT-generated path supervision for competing retrievers without sufficiently validating these adaptations or their training-budget comparability.

There are material evaluation inconsistencies. Appendix C.3 explicitly selects the graph checkpoint using test accuracy, compromising that reported generalization estimate. The claimed 80/20 Target-QA split is actually 300/63, and four-seed reporting is not clearly reconciled with five-run best-checkpoint selection. In Table 11, the 'w/o Graph' F1 of 0.5336 exceeds the arithmetic mean of its precision and recall, which is impossible under standard consistently averaged F1. Hit@k lacks a precise definition; its decrease from k=5 to k=10 suggests it is not conventional hit rate. These issues require correction before the results can be trusted.

The explanation evidence establishes plausibility rather than faithfulness. Disease-associated graph seeds and known interaction constraints already encourage disease enrichment. Ten examples rated with accompanying enrichment results, without matched baseline graphs or prediction-faithfulness tests, cannot establish that the generated graphs explain the model's decisions or identify cell-specific mechanisms.

Efficiency and reproducibility claims are stronger than the documentation supports. The complexity comparison omits explicit dependence on construction steps, rollout count/depth, repeated runs, and policy optimization, while providing no measured runtime or memory comparison. Important details such as the exact rule penalty and graph-selection criterion remain unclear. The claimed public resource links are blank in the supplied manuscript, so resource availability cannot be verified.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: combining multi-omic measurements, biomedical knowledge graphs, and language models for interpretable target prioritization.
The integration of incremental subgraph construction with classifier-based rewards and biological schema constraints is a promising methodological direction.

Reports improved aggregate Target-QA performance: F1 rises from 0.5094 for the task-tuned omics baseline to 0.5399 for GALAX. Similar results with Qwen provide evidence beyond one language-model backbone.
Evaluation includes cancer-type holdouts, external PedDep testing, modality and graph perturbations, reward-component ablations, and preliminary expert assessment of generated subgraphs.
weaknesses: The central reward lacks demonstrated mechanistic validity. A classifier trained to distinguish cancerous from non-cancerous samples is applied to generated partial graphs, but cancer classification confidence does not establish target essentiality, causal signaling, or intermediate reasoning correctness. Calibration on these partial graphs and independent validation of reward quality are missing; freezing the classifier does not prevent reward exploitation.

Equation 12 has an apparent optimization-sign error: minimizing negative reward times conventional cross-entropy decreases the probability of positively rewarded actions. This may be a notation error, but the implemented objective must be clarified because it governs the core algorithm.

The evaluation does not adequately separate cell-specific prediction from learning broadly shared essential genes. Training-set gene-frequency, average-dependency, nearest-neighbor, and strong supervised numerical baselines are absent. Most gains arise from task-specific fine-tuning, while the added benefit of GALAX is comparatively modest. Matched second-stage fine-tuning with random or heuristic subgraphs would better isolate the proposed reasoning mechanism.

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence. Table 11 reports F1=0.5336 with precision=0.5314 and recall=0.5275 for the no-Graph ablation, which is incompatible with standard F1 under consistent averaging. Hit@k is insufficiently defined and figures instead label precision@k. The claimed 80/20 split is reported as 300/63, and four experimental seeds coexist with five-trial checkpoint-selection descriptions. Appendix C.3 explicitly selects the graph classifier checkpoint using test accuracy, compromising that test estimate.

Mechanistic explainability remains weakly established. Enrichment and ratings of ten examples assess biological relatedness, with evaluators also given enrichment results, rather than whether subgraphs faithfully explain predictions. There are no comparable baseline ratings or targeted graph-intervention tests. Disease-related seed selection also makes subsequent disease enrichment partly expected. Patient-specific therapeutic claims exceed evidence from cell-line essentiality prediction.

Generalization evidence is encouraging but incomplete. Cancer-type holdouts lack baseline comparisons, and the external evaluation does not document cell-line overlap checks against training data. PedDep F1 improves only from 0.2728 for GNN-RAG to 0.2901 for LLaMA-based GALAX, without paired significance analysis. Claims of superiority on every metric are overstated: its PedDep Hit@10 is below GNN-RAG.

The scalability argument omits important costs from repeated graph construction, simulated continuations, retries, and per-sample optimization. No measured runtime or memory comparison supports the claimed computational parity. Overall, the promising integration and positive results do not outweigh unresolved technical and evaluation issues at a selective conference.
